title: The Door Shut and the Waters Prevail
summary: Noah, his household, and the animals enter the ark; the LORD shuts the door, and a worldwide flood destroys all life on dry land.
historicalContext: Genesis 7 records the event that divides the early history of the world into two eras. Noah has finished the ark after the long season of warning and labor described in chapter 6, and he now stands in his six hundredth year, the last representative of the faithful line traced from Seth through Enoch and Methuselah. The narrative gives a precise year, month, and day for the onset of the waters, a habit of dating unusual in Genesis and sharply different from the timeless settings of ancient Near Eastern flood stories, where quarrelsome gods unleash a deluge they cannot control and a hero saves himself by cunning. Here one God judges a corrupted earth, warns in advance, provides a refuge, and closes its door with His own hand. Jesus and the apostles treat these days as real history and as a pattern for the final judgment (Matthew 24:37-39; 2 Peter 3:5-7).
literaryContext: The chapter stands at the center of the flood narrative of 6:9-9:29, which is built as a great mirror: seven days, seven days, forty days, and one hundred fifty days lead up to “God remembered Noah” (8:1), and the same spans unwind in reverse afterward. Chapter 7 is the descending half. It moves from divine command (vv. 1-4) to obedience (v. 5), tells the embarkation twice with increasing detail (vv. 6-9, 13-16), and dates the outbreak of the waters between the two accounts (vv. 10-12). The refrain “as God had commanded” binds the scenes, and the climax arrives in four Hebrew words: the LORD shut him in. The final paragraph (vv. 17-24) slows to a solemn crescendo of rising waters, repeated verbs, and the word “all,” as the language of Genesis 1 is run backward and creation sinks into the deep, leaving only Noah and those with him.
themes: Grace that calls the righteous into refuge
The clean and unclean distinction before Sinai
A historical, worldwide judgment that undoes creation
The closed door and the end of probation
A preserved remnant carried through the waters

outline.title: The Call to Enter the Ark
outline.summary: The LORD invites righteous Noah and his household into the ark, specifies clean and unclean animals, announces a final week before forty days of rain, and Noah obeys.

outline.title: Embarkation Before the Rain
outline.summary: In his six hundredth year Noah enters with his family as the animals come two by two, and after seven days the floodwaters arrive.

outline.title: The Deep Breaks Open and the Door Closes
outline.summary: On a dated day the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven open, the full company is named within the ark, and the LORD shuts Noah in.

outline.title: The Waters Prevail Over the Mountains
outline.summary: The rising flood lifts the ark and overtops every high hill under the whole heaven by fifteen cubits.

outline.title: All Flesh Dies; Noah Remains
outline.summary: Every breathing creature on dry land perishes, only those in the ark survive, and the waters hold their height for one hundred fifty days.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The long speech of chapter 6 closed with a one-line report of years of work: “Thus did Noah” (6:22). Now the LORD speaks again, and His first word is an invitation: “Come thou and all thy house into the ark.” The ark is finished, the food is stored, and nothing remains except to step inside. God does not say “Go” as though sending Noah away from Himself; He calls him toward the place where divine protection will surround him. The covenant name, the LORD, appears as God addresses the man with whom He has already pledged His covenant (6:18).

“For thee have I seen righteous before me.” The verb answers two earlier verses in which God looked at the earth and saw only wickedness (6:5) and corruption (6:12). Across a whole race whose thoughts were evil continually, the divine gaze rested on one man. His righteousness is “before me,” measured by God’s verdict rather than by public reputation, and “in this generation,” set against a particular age of moral collapse. The story has already told us where it began: “Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (6:8). Grace comes first in the narrative, and righteousness follows. Hebrews 11:7 calls Noah an heir “of the righteousness which is by faith.” Building the ark did not purchase his standing; it was the visible shape his trust took over many years.

“Thou and all thy house” uses a singular “thee” for the man and includes his family under his leadership. Scripture does not teach that one person’s faith saves another automatically; Ezekiel names Noah precisely to make the point that each answers for himself (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). Yet Noah’s faithfulness had shaped his home, and his sons had shared the labor and the warning. Peter counts the result: eight souls were saved by water (1 Peter 3:20).

This command also marks the end of a long season of patience. God had waited while the ark was being prepared (1 Peter 3:20), and every plank had preached. Jesus later pointed to these days as a picture of the generation before His return, when ordinary life continues and the warning goes unheeded (Matthew 24:37-39). The word “Come” still sounds in the gospel (Matthew 11:28; Revelation 22:17), and it is always spoken before the storm breaks.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes one who is in right relation to God and lives consistently with that relation. Here the LORD Himself confirms the narrator’s description of Noah in 6:9. The phrase “before me” locates the verdict in God’s sight, while the surrounding narrative roots it in grace (6:8). Hebrews reads Noah’s righteousness as the fruit of faith, the same pattern later seen in Abraham.

The ordinary verb for entering or coming, used here as a command. Its first use with the ark in 6:18 was a promise (“thou shalt come into the ark”); now the promise becomes a summons. The same verb recurs through the chapter as the household and the animals enter (vv. 7, 9, 13, 15, 16), tying the whole embarkation to God’s word.

verses.bibleText: Of every clean beast thou shalt take to thee by sevens, the male and his female: and of beasts that are not clean by two, the male and his female.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Chapter 6 had told Noah to bring two of every kind, male and female, so that each kind could survive (6:19-20). Now, on the eve of the flood, the LORD makes the instruction more precise. This is the familiar pattern of Hebrew narrative, which states a matter broadly and then fills in its particulars, as Genesis 2 fills in the sixth day of Genesis 1. The two commands do not compete. A pair was the minimum needed to preserve every kind; the clean animals were to come in greater number.

The striking feature is what God does not explain. He gives no list and no definition. “Every clean beast” assumes that Noah already knew which animals belonged to that class and which did not. The distinction between clean and unclean, therefore, did not begin at Sinai. Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 set it down in writing for Israel many centuries later, but here it is already known and acted on before Abraham, before Israel, and before the ceremonial system of the tabernacle. It belongs to the order God gave humanity from early times, connected with sacrifice from the days of Abel’s offering of the firstlings of his flock (4:4).

“By sevens” renders a doubled Hebrew number, literally “seven seven.” It can mean seven individuals of each clean kind or seven pairs. The added phrase “the male and his female” leans toward pairs, though some have reasoned that the seventh animal was set apart for the offering after the flood. Either way, the clean animals outnumbered the unclean. The reason becomes clear in chapter 8 and 9: Noah’s first act on the renewed earth is to offer “of every clean beast” on an altar (8:20), and with vegetation swept away God permits the eating of flesh (9:3). The surplus of clean animals made worship and survival possible without wiping out any clean kind.

The text calls the second group “not clean” rather than using the usual word for unclean, and these too are carried through the judgment. Their status concerns what may be offered and eaten, not their worth as creatures. The LORD preserves man and beast (Psalm 36:6), and His tender mercies are over all His works (Psalm 145:9). The distinction for diet stands, but it never implies contempt for anything God has made.

wordNotes.explanation: This is the first appearance in Scripture of the adjective “clean,” later used throughout Leviticus for animals fit for sacrifice and food and for persons fit to approach worship. Its sudden use here without explanation shows that the category was already understood. The contrasting phrase in this verse, “not clean,” avoids the common term for unclean, though the meaning is the same distinction later spelled out in the law.

The repeated numeral expresses distribution, “seven by seven.” Hebrew uses doubling this way elsewhere, as in “two and two” in 7:9. Whether seven animals or seven pairs are intended, the phrase guarantees more clean than unclean animals and anticipates their use in sacrifice and food after the flood.

verses.bibleText: Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The birds are included under the same proportion as the clean beasts: “by sevens, the male and the female.” The Greek Old Testament and the Samaritan text read “clean birds” here, which fits the context well, since the raven Noah later releases belongs among the unclean birds (8:7; Leviticus 11:15). The point of the command is the same as in verse 2: more of the clean, enough of every kind.

The purpose clause states God’s intention plainly: “to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.” The ark is a means of preservation before it is anything else. The word “seed” carries weight in Genesis. It has already appeared in the promise of a Seed who would crush the serpent (3:15), and it will soon describe Noah’s descendants with whom God makes covenant (9:9). Here it refers to the offspring of the creatures, yet the same purpose runs underneath: in the midst of judgment God is securing a future.

“Upon the face of all the earth” looks beyond the flood to a whole world repopulated. The animals that go into the ark carry the blessing of the fifth and sixth days, to be fruitful and multiply (1:22), across the waters into the new beginning (8:17). The God who notices the fall of a sparrow (Matthew 10:29) does not forget the birds when He judges the earth.

wordNotes.term: לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע (lechayyot zera) — to keep seed alive
wordNotes.explanation: The verb in the causative sense means to preserve alive or keep living, and zera, “seed,” here means offspring. The phrase echoes 6:19-20, where the animals come “to keep them alive.” Joseph later uses the same verb when he tells his brothers that God sent him ahead “to preserve life,” another rescue that secures a future through judgment.

verses.bibleText: For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For yet seven days.” God gives Noah one more week. The span recalls the week of creation (2:1-3) and shows that time was already being counted in sevens long before Sinai; the same weekly rhythm appears again when Noah waits seven days between sending out the birds (8:10, 12). The Creator who made the world in six days and rested on the seventh now allows a final week before He unmakes what corruption has ruined. These seven days were themselves a mercy, a last interval in which anyone who would might still come.

“I will cause it to rain upon the earth.” The form of the verb describes action about to happen, and the subject is God. The flood is presented as a divine act from the beginning (6:17), not an accident of nature that God merely tolerated. “Forty days and forty nights” names a long, complete period. The number recurs in Scripture at moments of testing and transition: Moses on the mount (Exodus 24:18), the spies in Canaan (Numbers 13:25), Nineveh’s warning (Jonah 3:4), and Jesus in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2).

“Every living substance that I have made will I destroy.” The verb is the one used in 6:7, to wipe out or blot out, as one wipes a dish clean or erases writing. The phrase “that I have made” states the ground of God’s right. He is not destroying something that belongs to another; He is the Maker reclaiming a work that has been spoiled (Jeremiah 18:6). The earth had already been corrupted by its inhabitants (6:11-12), and judgment confirms what sin had begun.

Taken together, the verse holds patience and certainty side by side. The day is fixed, the means is named, and the result is announced in advance. Peter makes the same pairing for the end of the age: the Lord is not slack concerning His promise, but His delay is longsuffering toward a world He does not want to perish (2 Peter 3:9).

wordNotes.explanation: A rare noun meaning that which stands or exists, from a root meaning to rise or stand up. It appears only here, in 7:23, and in Deuteronomy 11:6, where it describes everything that belonged to Dathan and Abiram swallowed by the earth. In the flood context it is one of the most comprehensive terms available, covering all living existence on the land.

The verb machah means to wipe away or erase. It is used of wiping a dish (2 Kings 21:13), of blotting a name from a book (Exodus 32:32-33), and of God blotting out transgressions (Psalm 51:1). Its use here repeats the announcement of 6:7 and pictures the earth’s surface being wiped clean.

verses.bibleText: And Noah did according unto all that the LORD commanded him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Noah did according unto all that the LORD commanded him.” This line repeats the refrain of 6:22, now with the covenant name. The first notice covered the decades of building; this one covers the final week of gathering and entering. In both places the narrator compresses an enormous labor into a single sentence, and the compression is the message. Genesis has no interest in Noah’s skill as a builder or his management of a floating menagerie. It wants the reader to see one thing: he did what God said.

The word “all” matters. Noah did not select the commands that seemed sensible and set aside the rest. He built to God’s dimensions, took the animals in God’s proportions, and entered at God’s time. This pattern of command and exact fulfillment recalls creation, where God spoke and “it was so” (1:7, 9), and it anticipates the building of the tabernacle, where Moses did “according to all that the LORD commanded him” (Exodus 40:16).

Such obedience grew from trust. Hebrews 11:7 says Noah acted “by faith,” warned of “things not seen as yet,” and “moved with fear.” He had nothing to go on but the word of God, and he staked everything on it while a whole generation saw no reason to do the same. Obedience did not replace faith; it was faith in motion (James 2:22). Jesus states the same connection: love for Him shows itself in keeping His commandments (John 14:15).

wordNotes.term: כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּהוּ יְהוָה (kekhol asher-tsivvahu YHWH) — according unto all that the LORD commanded him
wordNotes.explanation: The formula pairs the verb tsavah, to command, with the comprehensive kol, all. It becomes a standard description of faithful execution in the Pentateuch, especially in the tabernacle chapters. Applied to Noah, it presents him as a model of obedient faith long before the law was written on stone.

verses.bibleText: And Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Noah was six hundred years old.” The narrative pauses to anchor the event in time. The genealogy had noted that Noah was five hundred when his sons began to be born (5:32), and the closing note of his life will say he lived three hundred fifty years after the flood (9:28-29). The flood is placed within a real lifetime, measured by the same reckoning used for the patriarchs who follow.

This kind of dating sets Genesis apart from the flood traditions of the surrounding nations, which float in an undated mythic past. Scripture presents a datable event in human history. Jesus spoke of Noah and the flood as plainly as He spoke of Lot and Sodom (Luke 17:26-29), and His warning depends on the reality of what happened. “The flood of waters” uses a term reserved in the Old Testament for this one catastrophe.

wordNotes.explanation: Outside Genesis 6-11 this noun occurs only in Psalm 29:10, where the LORD “sitteth upon the flood” as King. It is a technical term for the great flood of Noah rather than a general word for any river overflow. The Greek Old Testament renders it kataklysmos, the word Jesus uses in Matthew 24:39.

verses.bibleText: And Noah went in, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him, into the ark, because of the waters of the flood.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With verse 7 the narrative turns from command to action. “And Noah went in, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons’ wives with him, into the ark.” The verb is singular, keeping Noah at the head of the procession, while “with him” gathers the family around him. The order matches every listing in the flood account: Noah, his sons, his wife, and the sons’ wives (6:18; 7:13; 8:18). The household that had shared his labor now shares his refuge.

The count is eight persons, as Peter later records (1 Peter 3:20). Each man has one wife. In a world where Lamech had boasted of two wives and of violence (4:19-24), the family of the faithful preserves the pattern of Eden, one man and one woman joined as one flesh (2:24). The new humanity will descend from households shaped by the Creator’s design.

“Because of the waters of the flood” reads literally “from before the face of the waters.” It is the language of escape, the same expression used of people fleeing from a threat. Noah enters the ark because he believes what is coming, though nothing in the sky yet shows it. Verse 10 places the arrival of the waters after the seven days, which suggests that the family went aboard with time still to run, and verse 13 confirms that by the day the deep broke open every one of them was inside.

The contrast with Lot is instructive. Warned of Sodom’s destruction, Lot lingered until the angels took him by the hand (19:16). Noah, “moved with fear” (Hebrews 11:7), did not wait for proof. Faith that has heard God’s warning acts while the weather is still fair, and to the onlooker such faith can look foolish right up until the hour it is vindicated.

wordNotes.term: מִפְּנֵי מֵי הַמַּבּוּל (mippene me hammabbul) — because of the waters of the flood
wordNotes.explanation: The compound preposition mippene, “from the face of,” commonly expresses fleeing from danger or acting under pressure of a threat. Jacob fears Esau with the same construction, and Moses flees “from the face of” Pharaoh. Here it presents Noah’s entry as a flight to safety before the waters that God had announced.

verses.bibleText: Of clean beasts, and of beasts that are not clean, and of fowls, and of every thing that creepeth upon the earth,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 8 lists the animals in four groups: clean beasts, beasts that are not clean, fowls, and “every thing that creepeth upon the earth.” The categories follow the language of creation, where God made cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth after their kind (1:24-25), and birds to fly above the earth (1:20). Every class of land and air creature is represented; none is left out.

Once again the text says “not clean” rather than “unclean,” the same careful wording as verse 2. The distinction stands, but both groups enter the refuge. The sea creatures are absent from the list, since the judgment falls on what lives on dry land (7:22).

wordNotes.explanation: The participle of ramas describes creatures that move close to the ground, including small animals and reptiles. It is the same word used on the sixth day of creation and in the grant of dominion to humanity, so its appearance here ties the ark’s passengers to the original created order.

verses.bibleText: There went in two and two unto Noah into the ark, the male and the female, as God had commanded Noah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“There went in two and two unto Noah into the ark.” The animals come to Noah; he does not have to hunt them down. God had said they would come (6:20), and they do. The scene recalls the second chapter, where God brought the creatures to Adam to see what he would call them (2:19). There the animals came to receive names from the first man; here they come to receive shelter from the man through whom life on earth will begin again.

“Two and two” describes the manner of entry, pair by pair, male with female. It does not cancel the larger number of clean animals in verse 2. The clean kinds came in their several pairs, the others in a single pair, but all came in the same orderly way, matched for the future increase of the earth.

The sight must have been extraordinary for those who watched. Wild and domestic creatures, birds and crawling things, moved toward the ark as though summoned. Isaiah later laments that “the ox knoweth his owner” while God’s people do not consider (Isaiah 1:3), and Jeremiah observes that the stork and the swallow keep their appointed times while Israel ignores the LORD’s judgment (Jeremiah 8:7). The animals at the ark answered their Creator’s call; the people who saw them did not.

The refrain returns: “as God had commanded Noah.” Each stage of the embarkation is marked as fulfillment of the divine word, so that the reader never loses sight of who is directing events.

wordNotes.term: שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם (shenayim shenayim) — two and two
wordNotes.explanation: The dual numeral is repeated to express distribution, “in pairs.” Because shenayim is already dual in form, it cannot be made plural, and the repetition serves to describe a succession of pairs. The phrase therefore fits the entry of many pairs of clean animals as well as single pairs of the others.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth.” Verse 4 had announced, “For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain.” Verse 10 reports that it happened exactly so. Noah had done according to all that the LORD commanded (v. 5); now the LORD does according to all that He said. The faithfulness runs both ways, and God’s side never fails.

The week between entry and the flood was a real test. The ark was full, the family was inside, and the sky gave no sign. Peter warns of scoffers who ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” because all things seem to continue as they were (2 Peter 3:3-4). God’s timing may appear slow to human watchers, yet the vision “will surely come, it will not tarry” (Habakkuk 2:3).

wordNotes.term: לְשִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים (leshivat hayyamim) — after seven days
wordNotes.explanation: The definite article, literally “the seven days,” points back to the specific week announced in verse 4. The preposition marks the completion of that period. The phrasing quietly underscores that the flood arrived on the very day God had set.

verses.bibleText: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month.” This is the most exact date yet given in Scripture, and its precision belongs to history rather than legend. Year, month, and day are tied to the life of a named man, and the dates continue through the account until the earth is dry (8:4, 5, 13, 14). Whether Noah’s year began in spring or autumn cannot now be known, but the narrative clearly intends a real calendar.

The day itself is unremarkable. It is not a feast or a season of special meaning. Judgment came on an ordinary day while people were eating, drinking, and marrying (Matthew 24:38-39). Paul describes the end the same way: when people say “Peace and safety,” sudden destruction comes (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

“The same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up.” The flood was not rain alone. Waters from beneath burst upward, and the verb “broken up” describes a splitting or cleaving open. At creation God had gathered the waters and set bounds for the deep (1:9; Proverbs 8:28-29); now those bounds give way. At the same moment “the windows of heaven were opened,” and the waters above poured down. The separation of the second day (1:6-8) and the gathering of the third (1:9-10) are reversed together, and the earth is driven back toward the watery state of 1:2. The language describes violent upheaval on a global scale, a breaking open of the earth’s own foundations along with a downpour from above.

The prophets would later draw on this picture of creation unraveling to describe the day of the LORD (Isaiah 24:18; Jeremiah 4:23-26). Yet the same God who opens the windows of heaven in judgment can open them in blessing (Malachi 3:10). The waters are His to release and His to restrain (8:2). Peter connects this verse with the coming judgment: the world that then was perished by water, and the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire (2 Peter 3:5-7). The certainty of the first is the guarantee of the second.

wordNotes.term: תְּהוֹם רַבָּה (tehom rabbah) — the great deep
wordNotes.explanation: Tehom is the deep of 1:2, the primeval waters over which the Spirit moved. With rabbah, “great,” the expression appears elsewhere only in poetry, describing the vast abyss God controls and divided at the Red Sea. The verb niveqeu, “were broken up,” means to split open or cleave, the same verb used for the dividing of the sea and for water bursting from the rock. The phrase presents subterranean waters surging up by God’s command.

wordNotes.term: אֲרֻבֹּת הַשָּׁמַיִם (arubbot hashshamayim) — the windows of heaven
wordNotes.explanation: Arubbah denotes an opening or lattice, such as a window or chimney vent. The expression is a vivid picture for torrential release from the sky, not a claim about literal shutters. Elsewhere it describes abundant provision and overflowing blessing, showing that the same sovereign action can bring judgment or bounty.

verses.bibleText: And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.” What God announced in verse 4 now begins. The earlier verse used the ordinary verb for sending rain; this verse uses a noun that often denotes a heavy, driving downpour. The forty days mark the period of falling rain; the waters would continue to prevail for one hundred fifty days in all (v. 24).

Genesis had earlier described the earth watered by a mist rising from the ground (2:5-6), so this is the first time Scripture shows rain actually falling. The gift that God later uses to water crops and fill hearts with gladness (Acts 14:17) here becomes the instrument of judgment. Rain is not a power in its own right. It falls at God’s word (Job 37:6) and stops when He commands (8:2).

The measured number speaks of control as well as severity. The judgment is enormous, yet it has a beginning and an end set by God. He determines how long the rain will fall, and He has already determined to remember those in the ark.

wordNotes.explanation: Geshem often denotes a heavy or abundant rain, as in the great rain that ended the drought in Elijah’s day and the overflowing shower of Ezekiel’s judgment oracle. Its use here, after the more general verb of verse 4, conveys the force of the downpour that accompanied the breaking of the deep.

verses.bibleText: In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah's wife, and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth.” The second account of the embarkation is fuller than the first. Verse 7 spoke of “his sons”; here they are named, and the count of “the three wives of his sons” is exact. The grammar may be read as “had entered,” summing up that on the very day the deep broke open the whole company was already within.

Naming the sons looks backward to 5:32 and 6:10 and forward to 9:18-19 and the table of nations in chapter 10. These three men are the bridge between the old world and the new. Of them “was the whole earth overspread” (9:19), and every people descends from this one family.

The phrase “selfsame day” marks memorable days in the Pentateuch. Abraham and his household were circumcised on the selfsame day (17:26), and on the selfsame day the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12:41, 51). Noah’s day of entry belongs to that company: a day of deliverance fixed by God.

wordNotes.term: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (beetsem hayyom hazzeh) — in the selfsame day
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in the bone of this day,” using etsem, bone, in the sense of essence or very substance. The idiom stresses that something happened on that exact day. It recurs at solemn moments, such as Abraham’s circumcision, the Exodus, and Moses’ ascent of Nebo to die.

verses.bibleText: They, and every beast after his kind, and all the cattle after their kind, and every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind, and every fowl after his kind, every bird of every sort.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list of animals that accompany the family repeats a single phrase four times: “after his kind,” “after their kind,” “after his kind,” “after his kind.” This is the vocabulary of the creation week, where plants and creatures were made each according to its kind (1:11-12, 21, 24-25). Inside the ark the ordered world of Genesis 1 is gathered and preserved, even as outside it creation is dissolving into the deep.

“Every fowl after his kind, every bird of every sort” closes the list with a flourish: literally “every bird, every wing.” The word “every” runs through these lines like a drumbeat. No category God made is forgotten. When the flood ends, these same creatures will leave the ark “after their kinds” (8:19) to fill the earth again.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun min refers to a kind or category of living thing, used in Genesis 1 and in the food laws of Leviticus 11. It describes the created groupings God made and preserved; it is a descriptive biblical term, not equivalent to a modern scientific species. Its repetition here links the ark’s passengers to the creation order.

wordNotes.term: כֹּל צִפּוֹר כָּל־כָּנָף (kol tsippor kol-kanaph) — every bird of every sort
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “every bird, every wing.” Tsippor is the common word for a small bird, and kanaph, wing, stands for any winged creature. The pairing is a comprehensive expression that leaves no flying creature outside the scope of preservation.

verses.bibleText: And they went in unto Noah into the ark, two and two of all flesh, wherein is the breath of life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they went in unto Noah into the ark, two and two of all flesh.” As in verse 9, the creatures come to Noah, and once more they come in pairs. The repetition is not careless. Hebrew narrative often slows down at its most important moments, retelling an event with added detail so that the reader dwells on it. Here the narrator lingers at the threshold of the ark, as though walking the reader through the procession one more time before the door closes.

The new element is the description “wherein is the breath of life.” The phrase first appeared in 6:17, where God announced that He would destroy all flesh “wherein is the breath of life, from under heaven.” The same words now describe those spared. What separates the two groups is not their nature. Both are flesh, both breathe the same breath. The difference is where they are: inside the ark or outside it.

The breath of life is God’s gift, never a possession the creature holds independently. Genesis 2:7 shows the first man becoming a living soul when God breathed into his nostrils. The psalmist says that when God takes away their breath, creatures die and return to their dust, and when He sends forth His Spirit, they are created (Psalm 104:29-30). Job confesses that the breath of all mankind is in God’s hand (Job 12:10). Every creature walking into the ark lived only because God sustained its breath, and every one of them would be kept alive through the coming year by the same mercy.

wordNotes.term: רוּחַ חַיִּים (ruach chayyim) — breath of life
wordNotes.explanation: Ruach can mean wind, breath, or spirit, and chayyim means life. Together they describe the animating breath that God gives to living creatures. The phrase is shared by humans and animals in the flood narrative, showing that life in every creature depends on God. It does not describe a separable, self-existent entity, but the life-giving breath that God imparts and withdraws.

verses.bibleText: And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him.” The procession closes with the same refrain heard in verse 9. “Male and female” recalls the creation of humanity (1:27) and points ahead to the renewed command to be fruitful (8:17; 9:1). The future of every kind is carried in these matched pairs.

Then comes the climax of the whole embarkation in three Hebrew words: “and the LORD shut him in.” After the general name God in the first half of the verse, the covenant name returns. The personal, promise-keeping LORD acts with His own hand. In the Babylonian flood story the hero closes the hatch of his boat himself; in Genesis, Noah does not secure his own safety. The God who designed the ark and called him into it now seals it.

The act has two faces. For those within, it is protection. The Hebrew says the LORD shut the door “behind him” or “on his behalf,” enclosing Noah in a refuge no wave could breach. Isaiah uses the same picture for God’s people in a time of judgment: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee... until the indignation be overpast” (Isaiah 26:20). Noah did not need to hold the door against the storm; God held it.

For those outside, the closed door meant that the time of invitation was over. For long years the ark had stood open while Noah preached righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). The narrative places the shutting before the full force of the waters, not after. Mercy had been offered fully, and when the door closed, it closed by the same hand that had held it open. Jesus used this image in His parable of the virgins: “they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). Scripture describes a moment before Christ’s return when every case is settled (Revelation 22:11).

Today the door stands open. Christ calls Himself the door, through whom anyone who enters will be saved (John 10:9), and He is the One who opens and no man shuts (Revelation 3:7). The closed ark warns against delay; the open door invites entrance now.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּסְגֹּר יְהוָה בַּעֲדוֹ (vayyisgor YHWH baado) — and the LORD shut him in
wordNotes.explanation: The verb sagar means to close or shut, used of doors and gates. The preposition baad, “behind” or “around,” often carries the sense of protection or on behalf of someone, as when the LORD is called a shield about the psalmist. The closing is thus both an enclosure for safety and a final sealing.

wordNotes.term: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה (zakhar uneqevah) — male and female
wordNotes.explanation: These are the same two words used for humanity in 1:27 and for the animals in 6:19. Their recurrence emphasizes that the ark preserves the means of new life according to the Creator’s design, ready for the renewed blessing of fruitfulness after the flood.

verses.bibleText: And the flood was forty days upon the earth; and the waters increased, and bare up the ark, and it was lift up above the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the flood was forty days upon the earth.” The final paragraph of the chapter begins by restating the forty days of verse 12, now using the special word for the flood itself. From here the narrator never steps inside the ark. The camera, so to speak, stays outside on the rising waters.

Three short clauses follow in sequence, each the result of the one before: “the waters increased,” they “bare up the ark,” and “it was lift up above the earth.” The waters that had been destroying everything beneath them now raise the vessel above it all. The same flood is death to the world and buoyancy to the ark. Nothing in the account mentions a sail, a rudder, or a crew. Noah built the ark as God directed, but he could not steer it; it was carried.

Peter draws on this scene when he says that eight souls “were saved by water” (1 Peter 3:20). The water that judged the old world bore the faithful into the new one. He then calls baptism a “like figure,” not because the water itself washes away sin, but because baptism is “the answer of a good conscience toward God” through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 3:21). As Noah’s family passed through the waters into a cleansed earth, the believer is buried with Christ and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4).

The promise of Isaiah 43:2 fits the ark well: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee.” The waters did not stop rising for Noah; God kept him above them.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּרְבּוּ הַמַּיִם (vayyirbu hammayim) — and the waters increased
wordNotes.explanation: The verb rabah, to become many or great, is the same verb used in the creation blessing, “be fruitful, and multiply” (1:22, 28). In a grim reversal, the waters now multiply while the creatures God blessed are being swept away. After the flood the blessing of multiplying returns to the living (8:17; 9:1).

This word appears only in the flood narrative and in the account of Moses’ infancy, where his mother places him in a tevah of bulrushes daubed with pitch. In both cases a sealed vessel preserves one whom God has chosen through waters that threaten death. It is a different word from the ark of the covenant (aron).

verses.bibleText: And the waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth; and the ark went upon the face of the waters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth.” A new verb enters the description. To “prevail” is the language of strength and victory, used when Israel prevailed over Amalek while Moses’ hands were lifted (Exodus 17:11). The waters are pictured almost as an army overrunning the land. This verb will be repeated four times in the closing paragraph (vv. 18, 19, 20, 24), and with each repetition the sense of overwhelming force grows.

“And the ark went upon the face of the waters.” Against this mounting power stands one small vessel moving across the surface. The expression “the face of the waters” recalls 1:2, where the Spirit of God moved over the face of the waters before the first creation. The same surface over which God brooded at the beginning now carries the ark that bears the seed of a new beginning.

The Psalms celebrate the LORD who is mightier than the noise of many waters (Psalm 93:3-4) and invite trust even though the waters roar and the mountains shake (Psalm 46:1-3). Noah’s experience gives those words their deepest background. The waters prevailed over the earth, but they did not prevail over the ark.

wordNotes.explanation: From gabar, to be strong or mighty, related to gibbor, mighty man or warrior. It often describes one side gaining the upper hand in conflict. Applied to the waters, it pictures the flood as a conquering force overwhelming the land. The same verb describes the waters’ height in verse 24.

verses.bibleText: And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth.” The intensity rises again. Verse 18 said the waters increased “greatly”; now the Hebrew doubles the word, “very, very,” and the reader feels the flood climbing. The result follows: “all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.”

The sentence is written to leave no room for a limited reading. It is not enough to say “all the high hills,” since “all” can sometimes be used loosely in Hebrew as in English. The writer adds “under the whole heaven,” an expression used elsewhere for the entire world: the nations under the whole heaven (Deuteronomy 2:25), the God who sees under the whole heaven (Job 28:24), and the Lord who owns whatever is under the whole heaven (Job 41:11). The doubled “all” functions almost as a superlative. Water also seeks its own level; it cannot pile up over the highest hills of one region while lower lands elsewhere stay dry. If the high hills under the whole heaven were covered, the whole earth was under water.

Some have proposed that the flood was a regional inundation in the Mesopotamian valley, described in universal terms from the viewpoint of those who lived there. The proposal is offered sincerely, but the text resists it at every point. A local flood would not require an ark built over many years to preserve every kind of land animal and bird; Noah could simply have moved. God’s promise that waters would never again destroy all flesh (9:11, 15) would be broken by every great regional flood since. And Peter states plainly that “the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished” (2 Peter 3:6). The flood of Genesis 7 was worldwide.

The height of the mountains before the flood is not stated. The earth that emerged afterward may have been greatly reshaped by the upheaval of the deep. Psalm 104:6 recalls the waters standing above the mountains, and the following verses describe them retreating to the place God appointed. The God who sets the boundaries of the sea (Job 38:8-11) had for a time removed them.

wordNotes.explanation: The adverb meod, “very” or “greatly,” is doubled to express the highest degree. Verse 18 used it once; verse 19 uses it twice, building a crescendo. The same doubled form describes God’s promise to multiply Abraham exceedingly and the growth of Israel in Egypt.

wordNotes.term: תַּחַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמָיִם (tachat kol-hashshamayim) — under the whole heaven
wordNotes.explanation: This phrase consistently expresses universality in the Old Testament, describing the whole extent of the world under God’s sight and rule. Its addition to “all the high hills” removes the possibility that only a local landscape is meant. Daniel uses it of a judgment unparalleled “under the whole heaven.”

verses.bibleText: Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail.” A cubit was roughly the length of a forearm, about eighteen inches, so fifteen cubits is something over twenty feet. The figure is precise and modest, the kind of detail one expects from a sober record rather than from a tale bent on exaggeration. The ark itself was thirty cubits high (6:15), and a vessel of that build might ride with about half its height below the waterline. Fifteen cubits above the highest ground would keep the ark from grounding while the waters held their crest.

“And the mountains were covered.” The statement repeats the end of verse 19, and the repetition is deliberate. Hebrew narrative slows at its peak, saying the same thing twice so that it registers fully. Every summit lay beneath the surface. The whole earth was again an expanse of water, as it had been when “darkness was upon the face of the deep” (1:2).

The verb “covered” reappears in the song of the sea after the Exodus: “The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone” (Exodus 15:5). Both events show the same God using the waters as His instrument, destroying the oppressor and delivering His people. Isaiah later recalls the flood as the background to God’s oath of steadfast love: as He swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so He swears that His kindness will not depart from His people (Isaiah 54:9-10).

The worldwide covering of the mountains also explains why the earth could be called a new world after the flood. The surface that emerged was not simply the old landscape rinsed clean. It had been submerged, broken open from beneath, and reshaped, and God would give it back to Noah as a fresh beginning.

wordNotes.explanation: The standard Hebrew measure of length, based on the distance from elbow to fingertip, about eighteen inches or forty-five centimeters. The same unit gives the ark’s dimensions in 6:15 and later the measurements of the tabernacle. Its use here gives the depth of the waters in concrete, measurable terms.

From kasah, to cover or conceal. The passive form stresses that the mountains were wholly hidden beneath the water. The same verb describes the Red Sea covering Pharaoh’s army and, in another sense, God covering sin.

verses.bibleText: And all flesh died that moved upon the earth, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of beast, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth, and every man:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all flesh died that moved upon the earth.” The announcement of 6:13, “The end of all flesh is come before me,” is now carried out. The verb chosen means to expire, to breathe one’s last. The narrator does not use a word for drowning, though that is how death came; he speaks of dying, the penalty that has shadowed the human story since the warning of 2:17.

The list that follows runs in the order of creation: fowl, cattle, beast, creeping thing, and finally man. Birds were made on the fifth day; land animals and humanity on the sixth (1:20-27). Genesis 1 built upward from the waters to the creature made in God’s image; Genesis 7 removes the same creatures in the same sequence, so that the reader watches creation being taken apart.

Human beings come last and briefly: “and every man.” After the long list of animals, two Hebrew words suffice. The creature given dominion over the earth, whose corruption filled the earth with violence (6:11-12), is the reason the judgment fell at all. The animals perished with humanity because their world had been entrusted to human care, and when that care failed, they shared its ruin. Paul says the whole creation was subjected to futility because of sin and still groans, waiting for the day of redemption (Romans 8:20-22).

The scene is meant to be sobering. Genesis does not linger over the suffering, but neither does it soften the outcome. The holiness that sent the flood is the same holiness that sent Christ to bear judgment in our place, so that those who believe should not perish (John 3:16).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb gava means to expire or perish, describing the moment of breathing one’s last. It is used of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when they died and were gathered to their people. Here it heads the account of mass death outside the ark, and verse 22 completes it with the more common verb for dying.

Basar, flesh, denotes living creatures in their mortality and frailty, human and animal alike. In the flood narrative the phrase appears repeatedly for those judged and those preserved. Isaiah uses it to contrast human weakness with the enduring word of God.

verses.bibleText: All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.” This verse restates verse 21 with a different emphasis. Where the previous verse listed the creatures, this one defines them by what they had: breath in the nostrils. The wording reaches back to Genesis 2:7, where “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.”

That earlier verse described life as the union of dust and divine breath. The person did not receive an immortal soul placed inside a body; the whole person became a living being when God gave the breath. Death, then, is the reversal of that act. The breath returns to God who gave it, and the body returns to the dust (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The psalmist says that when a man’s breath goes forth, he returns to his earth, and in that very day his thoughts perish (Psalm 146:4). Genesis 7 does not picture the drowned multitude continuing consciously in some other realm. It says they died. Scripture places the hope beyond death in the resurrection, when those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Daniel 12:2; John 5:28-29).

“Of all that was in the dry land” sets the limit of the judgment. The creatures of the sea were not included, since the flood’s target was life on the land where human corruption had spread. The term for dry land is the word later used for the dry ground on which Israel crossed the sea (Exodus 14:21). In the flood the dry land disappears; at the Exodus God makes dry land appear in the midst of the waters to save His people.

The repetition of death in verses 21 and 22, framed by two different verbs for dying, leaves no doubt about the outcome. Everything that breathed on land, apart from the ark, perished.

wordNotes.term: נִשְׁמַת־רוּחַ חַיִּים (nishmat-ruach chayyim) — the breath of life
wordNotes.explanation: This fuller phrase combines neshamah, the breath of Genesis 2:7, with ruach chayyim of 6:17 and 7:15. It describes the life-breath God gives and sustains in every creature that lives on land. When it is withdrawn, life ceases; Scripture presents it as God’s gift on loan rather than an independent, undying component of the person.

Charavah denotes ground that is dry, the opposite of water-covered land. It is used of the dry path through the Red Sea and through the Jordan. Here it identifies the sphere of the judgment: creatures that lived on land, not those in the seas.

verses.bibleText: And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground.” Verse 4 had announced, “every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth.” Verse 23 records the fulfillment in almost the same words. The rare term for “living substance” returns, and so does the verb meaning to wipe away. God said it, and it was done.

The list this time begins with man and ends with birds, reversing the order of verse 21. The effect is to bring humanity to the front just before the contrast that closes the verse. “They were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” The whole human race outside the ark is set against one man and his household. Hebrew uses passive verbs on both sides, “were destroyed” and “remained,” and the grammar points to the same truth as the closed door: both judgment and survival rest in God’s hands. Noah did not outlast the flood by strength or ingenuity. He remained because God kept him.

This is the first appearance of the remnant theme in Scripture. The verb for “remained” gives the noun later used for the faithful few who survive judgment and carry God’s purpose forward. Isaiah speaks of a remnant that will return to the mighty God (Isaiah 10:20-22), Paul of “a remnant according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5), and Revelation of the remnant who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus (Revelation 12:17). The remnant is always defined by grace and faithfulness, never by numbers.

The New Testament treats this verse as a pattern for the end. God “spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person” (2 Peter 2:5). Jesus said the flood “came, and destroyed them all,” and so it will be when the Son of man is revealed (Luke 17:27, 30). Peter adds that the present heavens and earth are kept in store for fire against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men (2 Peter 3:7). As the flood brought the wicked of that age to an end rather than preserving them in endless suffering, the final judgment will make a full end of sin and sinners (Malachi 4:1), and a cleansed earth will remain for the redeemed (2 Peter 3:13).

wordNotes.explanation: From shaar, to remain or be left over. The related noun sheerit, remnant, becomes a key term for the survivors whom God preserves through judgment. Its first use for human survival is here, describing Noah and his family. Joseph later speaks of God preserving a posterity, and the prophets develop the remnant as the faithful core of God’s people.

This restrictive particle draws a sharp boundary: only Noah and those with him. It places the entire weight of survival on the one refuge God had provided. Outside the ark there was no alternative way of escape, a point the apostles echo when they speak of salvation in no other name.

verses.bibleText: And the waters prevailed upon the earth an hundred and fifty days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the waters prevailed upon the earth an hundred and fifty days.” The verb of strength and victory appears for the fourth time, now naming the full length of the waters’ dominance. The one hundred fifty days include the forty days of rain. The flood began on the seventeenth day of the second month (7:11), and the ark rested on the seventeenth day of the seventh month (8:4), exactly five months later; five months of thirty days each give the one hundred fifty days of this verse.

The chapter ends with the waters at their height and no word yet of relief. For months the ark drifted over a silent, drowned world. Faith inside the ark was not only a matter of entering but of waiting. Noah had obeyed God through years of building; now he must trust God through months without any visible sign of change.

The silence is broken by the next verse: “And God remembered Noah” (8:1). That sentence stands at the center of the whole flood narrative, where the rising half turns into the falling half. The psalmist’s counsel suits this pause well: “Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart” (Psalm 27:14).

wordNotes.term: חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם (chamishshim umeat yom) — an hundred and fifty days
wordNotes.explanation: The figure reappears in 8:3 when the waters begin to abate, framing the period of the waters’ dominance. Its match with the dates in 7:11 and 8:4 indicates a reckoning by thirty-day months. The careful numbering of days shows God measuring the judgment exactly, neither shortening nor prolonging it beyond His purpose.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it mean that God, not Noah, closed the door of the ark?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God who judges a corrupted world also provides one refuge, calls His people into it by grace, keeps them safe through the judgment, and shuts the door when the time of mercy ends.
discussionQuestions: How does God’s seeing Noah as righteous in 7:1 contrast with what He saw in 6:5 and 6:12?
What does the command about clean animals reveal about what Noah already knew before the law at Sinai?
Why does the narrator repeat “as God had commanded” and tell the entry into the ark twice?
How do the details of verses 19-23 establish the flood as worldwide rather than regional?
Why do Jesus and Peter use the days of Noah to describe the end of the age?
commonMisunderstandings: Noah was not saved because his labor earned God’s favor; he found grace first, and his obedience was the fruit of faith.
The clean and unclean distinction did not begin with Moses; Noah knew it and acted on it centuries before Sinai.
The flood was not a local Mesopotamian inundation; the text insists that the highest hills under the whole heaven were covered and all land life outside the ark died.
The closed door was not arbitrary harshness; it came after long warning and patience, and it protected those inside.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep judgment and refuge together: the same waters that ended the old world carried the ark, and the same hand that closed the door secured those within.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: The invitation “Come” is still given before the storm; enter the refuge God has provided in Christ while the door stands open.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God judges sin in history and will judge it finally, yet before judgment He always provides a refuge and calls people into it by grace.
flow: The world before the flood was filled with violence and corruption, and God announced its end.
Through Noah’s preaching and long patience God warned and waited.
He invited Noah and his house to come into the one ark He had designed.
When the time of grace ended, the LORD shut the door, and the waters destroyed all outside.
Jesus says the end of this age will be like the days of Noah, so the invitation to come to Him is urgent today.
simpleIllustrations: A lifeboat helps no one who admires it from the deck of a sinking ship; safety belongs to those who step inside.
A door that seals a vessel shut is frightening to those outside but is the very thing that keeps the storm from those within.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you come into the refuge God has provided in Jesus while the door of mercy is still open?
cautions: Do not present the flood as myth or parable; Scripture treats it as history and builds its warnings on that history.
Do not portray God as eager to destroy; the narrative stresses warning, patience, and provision before judgment.
Do not use the closed door to frighten people into despair; it is offered as a reason to come now.

reflectionQuestions: Am I living by faith in God’s word even when the world around me sees no sign of what He has said?
Is my obedience complete, like Noah’s “according unto all,” or do I choose which commands to follow?
How is my faithfulness shaping the people in my own household?
Have I entered the refuge God has provided in Christ, or am I still admiring it from outside?
What does the certainty of a past worldwide judgment teach me about the certainty of Christ’s return?
